items.title: Japan core inflation soars to highest this year as energy subsidy expiry pushes up consumer prices
items.summary: The core inflation figure — which strips out prices of food — was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists.
items.body: Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy costs and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy. Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month. Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before, government data released on Friday showed. Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher prices brought about by the Iran war. Energy prices climbed 2.2% in October, a sharp spike from the 0.6% decline in September. Gas prices jumped 5.8% compared to the 2.4% rise the month before.

items.title: Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off
items.summary: Odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000, which were once north of 70%, are extremely low on platform Kalshi.
items.body: As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off , prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year. On platform Kalshi , speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%. Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too. The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.

items.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
items.summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
items.body: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week. The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high. The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

items.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
items.summary: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock…
items.body: As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut. Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile.

items.title: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
items.summary: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?
items.body: Mercedes-Benz 's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it. In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high. Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure." The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant. Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.

items.title: Christine Lagarde: Acting in time
items.body: It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last. In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market. But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere. For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding. Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top.

items.title: Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens 'tremendous tax'
items.summary: Trump spoke at the White House after meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a historic trilateral summit in China.
items.body: President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so. "We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff. "I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here." Trump's latest push for more data-center construction in the U.S. came despite Americans repeatedly stating — and showing with their votes — that they dislike the structures. CNBC's All-America Economic Survey found that 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% of respondents said they would support one.

items.title: As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive
items.summary: Anthropic options list Monday. They will likely be expensive
items.body: As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list. If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading. A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago. Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

items.summary: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
items.body: The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times. In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports. And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move. The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

items.title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
items.summary: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an…
items.body: Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan , which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost. In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

items.title: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
items.summary: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.
items.body: Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets. The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members. This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million). The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful." " Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said. At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

items.title: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
items.summary: Cybersecurity companies have been hunting for acquisitions in the AI era.
items.body: Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%. The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion. Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.

items.body: Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds. Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm. "We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's " Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business. Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

items.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
items.summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
items.body: Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so. "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time. Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction. Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in. "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

items.title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey
items.summary: UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey…
items.body: The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn. In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent Treasury watchdog, said the latest figures were “broadly in line” with its October forecast for a £1.1bn fall in total borrowing for the 2026-27 financial year.

items.body: SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC has learned. Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5. It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington . The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.

items.title: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?
items.summary: Technology stocks tanked despite one of the most hotly anticipated tech IPOs in years. Why Anthropic couldn't revive AI animal spirits.
items.body: Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175. Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls. Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

items.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
items.summary: People stocking up on long-life food drove retail sales higher October, according to official data.
items.body: Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures. Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said. The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks. Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying . The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes. Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.

items.title: What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
items.summary: The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees issue unresolved, says No 10 After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a…
items.body: After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed? The two sides have struck three deals long expected from this summit: food and drink, emissions trading and a youth exchange programme. The food and drink deal will ease Brexit controls on the vast majority of animal and plant products being traded between Britain and the EU, a boon for producers of meat, dairy, wine and flowers among many other products. If all goes well – and there is still an if – the deal will apply from 1 March 2028. The energy deal relinks the British and EU emissions trading schemes, shielding industrial producers on both sides from levies on polluting products, such as steel and fertilisers, as well as electricity. This should enter into force in 2028.

items.title: Trump says he discussed Jensen Huang with Xi; Bessent tells CNBC Nvidia chip export policy is unchanged
items.summary: Trump said he discussed Jensen Huang with China's Xi. Bessent said the ousted Nvidia CEO didn't come up in talks he had while in China.
items.body: President Donald Trump on Friday said he and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed their shared affinity for former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during their talks in China this week. Earlier in the day, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the ousted leader was not mentioned in separate talks he had with Chinese officials. "I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, 'Oh, brilliant, brilliant! He's a brilliant man.' He is," Trump said at a White House press conference. Asked earlier Friday on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" if Huang, a close ally of Trump 's, had come up in "any of your discussions with the Chinese," Bessent said "no," without elaborating. A senior Trump administration official later said that both Trump's and Bessent's remarks were correct, and that both were addressing their own conversations.

items.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
items.summary: Eating at your desk? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
items.body: There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's. Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish. From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive. "We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah. She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left". Casey, a content creator for an energy company, says he used to eat tuna at his desk but has since "reformed". He says you have to "suss out the smelliness" and then decide if it's acceptable to eat at the desk.

items.title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
items.summary: News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations…
items.body: A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged. An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable. News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries. Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran .

items.title: The bull market has a new problem. The 'smart money' is selling
items.summary: Companies are shifting from share buybacks to stock issuance, adding new supply. Anthropic’s $81 billion IPO puts that demand to the test.
items.body: Companies have shifted from buying back shares to issuing them, adding to the supply that the four-year-old bull market must absorb. "No matter how you measure it, U.S. corporations have changed their behavior over the past two years, switching from repurchasing in 2024 to issuing today," Acadian Asset Management portfolio manager Owen Lamont wrote in a letter to investors this month. "The question you should be asking is: Why is the smart money selling?" As of late last week, net new issuance of shares equaled 3.1% of total market capitalization, according to a recent Acadian analysis. While net issuance remains below the peaks during the tech bubble and the covid bubble, the analysis shows that the era of repurchases has ended and an era of equity issuance has begun. And more supply came to the market this week with Anthropic 's blockbuster IPO.

items.summary: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.
items.body: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force. Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason. Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all". But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers. The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed. Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

items.title: ‘Gloucestershire nouveau’: UK vineyard uncorks its 2026 answer to beaujolais
items.summary: Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years Forget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s…
items.body: F orget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest. Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine. The First Release is what the vineyard calls its “Gloucestershire nouveau” – its tongue-in-cheek nod to beaujolais nouveau, a young, fruity red that is released on the third Thursday in November . Beaujolais nouveau was traditionally made for local consumption and was a way for workers and villages to enjoy the first sip of that year’s harvest. Vines were first planted on the Gloucestershire site of a fruit farm in 1973, while Three Choirs has been bottling a young wine every November since the 1980s.

items.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
items.summary: Rockstar Games ended a 13-year wait with what is expected to be the biggest entertainment launch ever.
items.body: Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to be the biggest entertainment launch in history after the blockbuster video game debuted on Thursday , following a 13-year wait. Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch. New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access . Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than 24.5 million units, making about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics site Sensor Tower. In comparison, this year's highest-grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas . GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both firms for comment.

items.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
items.summary: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government…
items.body: Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency. The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September , which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.

items.title: ‘More than just a game’: How GTA VI’s blockbuster launch fuels a booming content economy
items.summary: GTA VI’s blockbuster launch is creating a wider economy around livestreams, social clips and high-volume content farms as millions tune in to watch others play.
items.body: Grand Theft Auto VI has exploded out of the gate after a 13-year wait, drawing millions of buyers while fueling a parallel economy of livestreams, clips and other content built around people watching the game as much as playing it. GTA VI has delivered a blockbuster debut , with about 19.1 million copies sold — including preorders — by Thursday morning, representing roughly $1.84 billion in sales, according to Sensor Tower. The GTA franchise itself has sold more than 470 million units worldwide. Take-Two Interactive , which owns the studio behind the game, has not yet disclosed a profit figure for the title. Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" that he sees further upside for Take-Two, which his firm holds in its portfolio. "It's crazy good.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity. items.title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death of woman at Somerset holiday park
items.summary: Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun…
items.body: The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset . Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory. Wendy Jones, 68, a grandmother from Hereford, was sitting in her mobility scooter for bingo with about 100 others when the ceiling collapsed. She was among six guests to be treated in hospital after the incident and died six months later. A postmortem examination revealed a clear link between the injuries she suffered and her subsequent death.

items.title: Forget Anthropic: In Europe, the IPO hype is about a blue lagoon
items.summary: Iceland’s famed Blue Lagoon geothermal spa is going public in a $110 million IPO, tapping investor interest in tourism and the booming wellness industry.
items.body: While investors are fixated on Anthropic's blockbuster stock market debut , a very different IPO is making waves in Europe: Iceland's Blue Lagoon, the operator of one of the world's most famous geothermal spas. Blue Lagoon Corp. raised roughly 14.3 billion Icelandic kronur ($110 million) through the offering, valuing the Icelandic geothermal spa operator at about $787 million, according to the company's investor presentation . The Blue Lagoon traces its origins to 1992, when Blue Lagoon Ltd. was founded to study the water in the Blue Lagoon, an open-air pool of warm, milky-blue water set in a black lava field in southwestern Iceland. It grew into a business spanning a spa, hotels and skincare made with ingredients from the lagoon.

items.body: A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned. Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage. France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies . It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix. In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary: It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at…
items.body: A ndy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform.

items.title: Warsh wants Fed officials to talk less. Instead, they’re talking more
items.summary: Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately while the Fed chairman stays on the sidelines.
items.body: In his first six months as Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh has diligently avoided signaling where he sees monetary policy and interest rates headed. His colleagues have been only too happy to fill the void. Fed officials have been rushing to the microphones lately, voicing sometimes conflicting opinions on how the central bank should be handling an inflation bug that the economy can't seem to shake. Most agree that rates should be raised — and soon. Some are willing to hike at a measured pace as conditions play out, while others, such as Governor Christopher Waller and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem , entertain the thought of more aggressive hikes in a shorter period of time.

items.body: California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang. The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday. Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it…
items.body: A I is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. The World Economic Forum finds analytical thinking is now the skill employers value most, and estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training to adapt to this shift by 2030.

items.title: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'

items.body: Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra : "It's going to be tough." He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014. Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence , vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles. "It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview.

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary: Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an…
items.body: I t’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense.

items.summary: Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams. Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines…
items.body: Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack. But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked , spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries . Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever.

items.title: Data center construction costs soar 13% in 2026

items.body: A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox. The demand for large-scale data centers in the U.S. this year, driven by the need for computing power for artificial intelligence, grew well beyond the supply of powered land and the labor to build these structures. items.summary: More than two thirds of respondents reported noticing rises in the cost of living.
items.body: There has been "a major increase" in the overall cost of living in the past 12 months in Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man, a survey has found. Island Global Research, a market research and consultancy company, found more than 69% of respondents in Jersey, 68% in Guernsey and 70% in the Isle of Man said they had noticed a cost increase , external . The survey, which was completed by over 1,000 people in each island, saw 57% of respondents describe themselves as "less than comfortable" with about one in 10 going without essentials like food and heating. The survey also found 65% said they now spent less on non essentials and 53% said they are shopping around more because of the price rises. In Jersey, 10% of respondents reported they could not afford the increased costs and often have to go with out essentials, while in Guernsey it was 11%.

items.title: How to get a bigger Black Friday bargain: cashback, price matches and gift cards
items.summary: From cashback on what you buy to cut-price gift cards, we offer tips on how to maximise savings on your shopping With Black Friday on the horizon, retailers are already offering discounts, and over the next few weeks you can expect to see more price cuts as they attempt to…
items.body: With Black Friday on the horizon, retailers are already offering discounts, and over the next few weeks you can expect to see more price cuts as they attempt to entice us to open our wallets. It could be a great time to snap up the things on your Christmas list or buy household items you need yourself. And there are ways to maximise your savings on Black Friday – which this year falls on 27 November – by doubling up on discounts, or earning cashback on your purchases. Assuming you have shopped around for a good price and are sure you really want what you are about to buy, here are some ways you can make the bargain even better. Some of the big banks pay cashback on purchases made with their debit cards, with offers linked to specific retailers. Lloyds, for example, runs the Rewards programme, which has cashback deals with a rolling cast of retailers.

items.title: AI is changing software engineering — and some developers miss the struggle
items.summary: AI coding tools are making software engineers faster, but developers tell CNBC the work has lost its "sense of joy and fun."
items.body: When Gemma Rodgers began her computer science degree in 2002, software engineering was seen as a future-proof and lucrative career. It appealed to people who enjoyed getting into the weeds of code, tracking down bugs and building programs from scratch. It's an industry that has always moved fast, Rodgers, a software developer based in the U.K., told CNBC. But the arrival of artificial intelligence has accelerated the pace, with AI tools now part of the daily work of every software engineer she knows. In a 2026 Stack Overflow survey , 83% of software developer respondents said they use at least one AI tool. As AI coding tools help engineers write, debug and test code faster than ever, some are mourning the job they used to have.

items.title: These US fishers see offshore wind as a ‘godsend’. Trump wants to shut it down
items.summary: Despite the president’s attacks, Sea Services is training New England fishers in offshore wind construction and providing them with a second income stream On a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts.…
items.body: O n a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island. “God forbid, if anybody was to fall, we could be there to help them out,” said Capt Kevin Souza, who has a bulldog tattoo on his shin to mark his time in the navy. Souza and his three-man crew were fishers by trade, but this trip was different. Instead of fishing, they were working for Sea Services North America, a co-op funded through contracts with offshore wind developers. It was welcome work for these fishers who weather a legally restricted scalloping season.

items.title: Lagarde says EU funds should take first losses on chip plants, data centers
items.summary: Public funds should absorb early risks in major technology projects, the European Central Bank chief said Friday.
items.body: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said Friday that EU public funds should take the first losses on major chip-plant and data-center projects to help attract private capital. "Where we agree that a challenge requires a European solution, we should strengthen the European institutions that can provide it," she said in her final address to the Frankfurt European Banking Congress before she steps down as head of the ECB in February.

items.title: Japan Tobacco shares fall 10%; Russia seizure hits 900,000 investors
items.body: TOKYO -- Shares in Japan Tobacco plummeted 10% on Friday after the company said it expects to post its largest net loss on record and cut its dividend forecast after losing control of its Russian operations.
